title: When you are not well
goal: Say what hurts, buy medicine, see a doctor and ask for help in an emergency — the unit you hope not to need and will be very glad to have.
bekal: name the parts of the body and say which one hurts
describe symptoms at a pharmacy or a clinic
call for help, and understand what is asked of you

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Di apotek
dialogs.intro: Sarah has not slept well and her stomach is not right. She goes to the pharmacy on the corner.

notes: **Sakit + body part is the whole grammar of pain.** *Sakit perut* (stomach ache), *sakit kepala* (headache), *sakit gigi* (toothache). No verb, no preposition. And *Saya sakit* on its own means "I'm ill".
**Sejak means "since" and takes a point in time**: *sejak kemarin*, *sejak pagi*, *sejak minggu lalu*. Its partner *selama* means "for (a length of time)": *selama tiga hari*.

**Ada yang bisa dibantu?** is the standard shop and office greeting — literally "is there something that can be helped?". It uses the passive *dibantu*, which is why it sounds odd word-for-word. Recognise it as a fixed phrase.

**Pharmacies do a lot of the work of a doctor in Indonesia.** An *apotek* will listen to your symptoms and sell you something appropriate, and many stock antibiotics that would need a prescription elsewhere. For anything serious, or a fever that lasts, go to a *klinik* or *rumah sakit* — and if you are in Indonesia for a while, know where the nearest one is before you need it.

**Demam berdarah** (dengue fever) is the one to take seriously: high fever, aching behind the eyes, and it is spread by daytime mosquitoes. Any fever lasting more than two days deserves a blood test rather than another packet from the pharmacy.

grammars.title: The body
body: You need these mainly to point and name; nobody expects grammar from a person in pain.
after: ⚠️ *Tangan* covers hand **and** arm; *kaki* covers foot **and** leg. Indonesian simply does not split them, and if the distinction matters you say *telapak tangan* (palm) or *lengan* (upper arm).

grammars.title: Symptoms and states
body: All of these are adjectives, so no verb is needed: *Saya demam* is a complete sentence.
after: **Pusing is not quite "dizzy".** It covers the whole family of head trouble — light-headedness, a dull headache, and figuratively being overwhelmed. *Saya pusing* said about work means "my head is spinning with all this".

**Masuk angin** deserves its own line. Literally "wind entered", it is a very Indonesian complaint covering bloating, chills and general malaise, and its traditional treatment is *kerokan* — coining the back with a coin until it reddens. You will meet both, and both are taken entirely seriously.

head: Indonesian
English
rows: I'd like to see a doctor.
I've had a headache since yesterday.
I take this medicine every day.
How many days should I rest?

blocks.text: *Minum obat* — literally "to drink medicine" — is how Indonesian says "to take medicine", even for tablets. Never *makan obat*.

Practical note: many clinics and hospitals want your *asuransi* (insurance) details or payment up front, and travel insurance documents are worth having on your phone. The word for a receipt you can claim on is *kuitansi*.
Learn these as whole blocks. In an emergency nobody assembles grammar.
The national emergency number is **112**, which works from any phone. Police is 110 and ambulance 118, but 112 will get you all of them.

*Kehilangan* ("to lose") and *dicuri* ("to be stolen") are both built from roots you can now see: *hilang* (gone, missing) wrapped in *ke-…-an*, and *curi* (steal) with the passive *di-*. Even in a crisis, the language keeps its shape.
